comparison: Both strongly support the finding that cholinergic axons signal locomotion state in a binary manner (C2, C68-C94, C149-C150, C183). OpenEval provides detailed technical analysis of calcium imaging and GRAB-ACh measurements, while peer reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding across all three reviewers with direct quotes confirming binary locomotion signaling regardless of velocity.

Perfect agreement on lack of cholinergic responses to visual stimuli and visuomotor mismatch (C3-C4, C77-C78, C81-C82). Both evaluations accept the negative findings with OpenEval emphasizing hemodynamic artifact controls and peer reviewers explicitly confirming 'Cholinergic axons did not seem to respond to grating stimuli or visuomotor prediction error.'

Both support the validation of calcium imaging with GRAB-ACh measurements (C79-C80, C83). OpenEval emphasizes this as critical methodological validation, while peer reviewers implicitly accept this correspondence as foundational to the study's methodology without questioning the calcium-to-acetylcholine inference.

Both support the latency analysis showing cholinergic activation follows layer 2/3 responses (C73-C75, C128). OpenEval provides detailed analysis of temporal ordering as evidence against cholinergic drive of initial responses, while peer reviewers implicitly accept this timing analysis as foundational to the binary locomotion signal finding.

Both support the correlation analyses across behavioral variables (C95-C100). OpenEval details systematic comparisons showing locomotion as primary correlate with controls for ceiling effects, while peer reviewers implicitly accept these control comparisons as supporting the robustness of the locomotion-cholinergic correlation.

Perfect agreement on lack of direct cholinergic activation of neurons (C5, C125-C128). OpenEval emphasizes optogenetic evidence showing no calcium activity increase, while peer reviewers implicitly accept this through noting that cholinergic effects only occur when paired with stimuli, not in isolation.

Strong agreement on layer-specific optogenetic effects (C6-C8, C103-C113, C118, C151, C170). OpenEval provides detailed analysis of controls for locomotion velocity changes and stimulation artifacts, while all three peer reviewers explicitly affirm the differential modulation of layer 5 vs layer 2/3 responses to both bottom-up and top-down inputs.

Both support the finding that optogenetic stimulation shows saturation effects during locomotion for grating responses but not mismatch responses (C109, C114-C115, C119). OpenEval interprets this as acetylcholine being one component among multiple factors, while peer reviewers accept the partial explanation and multiplicative vs. additive gain analysis.

Both support the distinction between locomotion effects (multiplicative and additive) and cholinergic effects (primarily multiplicative) on orientation tuning (C116-C117). OpenEval notes this as important mechanistic insight while suggesting more detailed statistical characterization needed, peer reviewers accept this nuanced finding as part of the incomplete explanation.

Strong agreement on acetylcholine's causal role in decorrelation (C10, C129-C143, C152-C153, C155, C171, C185). OpenEval emphasizes convergent evidence from optogenetic and chemogenetic approaches with layer-specific effects, while all three peer reviewers explicitly affirm the decorrelation finding with bidirectional chemogenetic validation.

Perfect agreement on differential decorrelation effects based on baseline correlation (C135-C136). OpenEval describes this as important mechanistic detail showing non-uniform effects, while peer reviewers implicitly accept this nuanced observation as part of the overall decorrelation finding.

Perfect agreement on behavioral effects during chemogenetic experiments (C137-C138). OpenEval notes this as important control that complicates interpretation but strengthens causal link, while peer reviewers implicitly accept these behavioral effects without suggesting they confound neural findings.

Both support layer-specific effects on response latency (C8, C144-C148). OpenEval emphasizes this as novel finding complementing amplitude effects with optogenetic recapitulation of locomotion effects, while peer reviewers accept the layer 5 latency reduction as part of the broader layer-specific modulation pattern.

Both support the lack of latency effects in layer 2/3 (C145, C147). OpenEval notes consistency with other layer-specific findings, while peer reviewers explicitly confirm the differential effect stating cholinergic input affects 'layer 5 excitatory neurons, but not layer 2/3 neurons.'

Both support the interpretive conclusion that acetylcholine enhances responsiveness to external inputs (C11, C156, C184). OpenEval marks this as reasonable inference rather than directly demonstrated result, while peer reviewers implicitly accept this interpretation through affirming the underlying data as 'convincing' without challenging the mechanistic proposal.

Both accept speculative interpretations about plasticity gating, movement state signaling, and consciousness (C12, C165, C168, C175, C180, C186-C187). OpenEval explicitly marks these as SPECULATION requiring additional validation, while peer reviewers implicitly accept these as reasonable hypotheses by describing experiments as 'well-executed' and 'rigorous' without challenging the speculative discussion.

Both accept the adequacy of control experiments for optogenetic stimulation (C105-C107). OpenEval details controls for locomotion velocity changes and stimulation artifacts as appropriate, while peer reviewers implicitly accept controls by describing experiments as 'well executed' with 'high quality' data without questioning alternative explanations.

OpenEval identifies methodological considerations and potential confounds (C157-C160) including antidromic activation concerns and projection specificity arguments. These caveats are marked as UNCERTAIN by OpenEval but are not explicitly addressed in peer review evaluations, suggesting peer reviewers either did not identify these concerns or considered them adequately addressed.

OpenEval explicitly acknowledges sampling bias limitations (C161-C164) regarding neuronal populations sampled, noting distinct properties of undersampled populations. Peer reviewers do not explicitly discuss these sampling limitations, though OpenEval notes they do not invalidate main conclusions.

Both address theoretical frameworks and speculative interpretations (C169, C172-C177, C181-C182). OpenEval marks these as UNCERTAIN, noting attractor dynamics and predictive processing hypotheses are speculative but consistent with data, while peer reviewers implicitly accept these theoretical discussions without challenge as part of well-executed research.

OpenEval systematically catalogs citations establishing scientific context (C13-C67, C72, C101, C120-C124, C166-C167, C178-C179). These are marked as SUPPORTED as accurate representations of prior literature. Peer reviewers do not explicitly evaluate individual citations but implicitly accept the contextual framing through their overall positive assessments.
